stem: A client exercising in extreme heat has a core temperature of 40.5°C (104.9°F) and new confusion. Which heat-related illness should the nurse suspect?
rationale: CDC/NIOSH identifies heat stroke as the most serious heat-related illness and lists very high body temperature together with confusion or altered mental status among its characteristic findings. This presentation therefore indicates heat stroke and requires emergency treatment and rapid cooling. Heat exhaustion more typically causes heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, thirst, and elevated temperature without the defining severe central nervous system dysfunction of heat stroke. Heat syncope is a brief fainting or dizziness episode, and heat cramps are painful muscle spasms. Therefore B is uniquely correct.
educational_objective: Recognize very high core temperature with new central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion as heat stroke rather than less severe heat-related illnesses.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
source_locator: Heat Stroke: most serious heat-related illness; symptoms include confusion/altered mental status and very high body temperature; emergency treatment and rapid cooling are required. Heat Exhaustion, Heat Syncope, and Heat Cramps sections provide the contrasting symptom patterns.
source_claim_supported: Very high body temperature accompanied by confusion or altered mental status strongly indicates heat stroke and requires emergency care; heat exhaustion, heat syncope, and heat cramps have different clinical patterns.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.46 and Medical Emergencies/Pathophysiology content: manage clients with acute or life-threatening physical health conditions, recognize complications, perform emergency care, and intervene for acute physiologic instability.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — heat stroke recognition and emergency response

source_original.stem: A client exercising in extreme heat has a core temperature of 40.5°C (104.9°F) and confusion. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.D: A normal response to strenuous exercise.

source_original.rationale: Very high core temperature accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion is characteristic of heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency requiring rapid cooling and emergency care. Option B is correct. Heat exhaustion and uncomplicated dehydration do not account for this severe hyperthermia with altered mental status.
source_original.source_detail: Heat Stroke section: very high body temperature with central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, altered mental status or loss of consciousness is a medical emergency requiring emergency services and rapid cooling. CDC/NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses page updated 2026-03-03; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the heat-stroke construct and key B. Replaced two weak/nonparallel distractors with CDC-listed heat syncope and heat cramps, clarified that confusion is new, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct recognition pattern using realistic heat-illness differentials.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current CDC/NIOSH heat-stress guidance; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC/NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses > Heat Stroke, with Heat Exhaustion, Heat Syncope, and Heat Cramps sections for differential distractors
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the directly supported combination of very high body temperature and altered mental status/confusion for heat stroke and does not rely on sweating status or another nonessential criterion.

distractor_audit.A: Heat exhaustion can cause weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea and elevated temperature but does not best explain severe hyperthermia with new CNS dysfunction.
distractor_audit.C: Heat syncope is characterized by brief fainting/dizziness rather than this severe hyperthermia-plus-confusion pattern.
distractor_audit.D: Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms and do not explain the CNS dysfunction and very high core temperature.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only heat stroke accounts for both the very high core temperature and new confusion in this heat-exposure setting.
audit_findings.cueing: All four options are recognized heat-related illnesses and are parallel diagnostic labels.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — acute life-threatening environmental illness recognition and emergency response.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current CDC/NIOSH Heat Stroke and differential sections, all alternatives, rationale, objective, NCSBN Physiological Adaptation mapping, ambiguity and cueing. B remained uniquely correct.
